title: Time… a programmer's worst enemy // The Code Report
text: Time is a programmer's worst enemy because real-world timekeeping is chaotic: the Earth rotates unevenly (requiring leap seconds), time zones have arbitrary offsets including half-hour and quarter-hour variations plus daylight savings complications, and the Gregorian calendar inconsistently assigns 28–31 days to different months. JavaScript's Date API, inherited from Java in 1995, is universally hated and makes working with dates and time zones unnecessarily painful. The proposed Temporal API aims to fix this by providing time-zone-aware objects and finer time precision (microseconds, nanoseconds). Eliminating daylight savings would ironically force programmers who've already buried themselves in complex time-handling code to update legacy systems all over again.

title: Ist die Zukunft schon Vergangenheit? – Das Zeit-Paradox
text: According to relativity's "block universe" model, yes—your past, present, and future all exist simultaneously and equally in spacetime; different observers experience different "nows" depending on their motion through space, suggesting all moments are equally real. However, quantum mechanics complicates this: since quantum processes are fundamentally random and unpredictable, the future cannot be completely predetermined, suggesting a "growing block" model where time genuinely moves forward as quantum events occur. The video presents three competing models of time but concludes that physicists don't actually know which one is correct. The transcript covers the implications for free will, the nature of "now," and the question of whether the future is predetermined or still open.

title: Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT
text:
# How LLMs Like ChatGPT Are Built

ChatGPT is trained in three stages—downloading and predicting text from the internet, imitating human-labeled conversations, then discovering better solutions through trial and error—each progressively cheaper and more interesting than the last.

## Pre-training: Internet as a textbook
**44 terabytes, not petabytes.** FineWeb (the dataset training models like GPT-4) compresses the entire useful internet into 44TB—fits on a modern hard drive. Common Crawl (2.7 billion web pages) is aggressively filtered: malware/spam blocked, HTML stripped to text only, non-English purged, duplicates removed, personally identifiable info scraped.

**GPT-4 sees 100,277 atomic chunks.** Tokenization isn't character-by-character; "hello world" = 2 tokens, but "hello world" (lowercase) = 3 tokens. Case matters. Byte-pair encoding groups common symbol pairs (e.g., "th" + "e" → single token) to shrink sequences. Tokens are random IDs the model never "understands"—they're just unique symbols.

**Pre-training takes 3 months on thousands of GPUs. Post-training takes 3 hours.** One GPU does supervised fine-tuning because conversation datasets (millions vs. 15 trillion tokens) are tiny. This is why GPT-4 training cost millions; GPT-2 reproduction costs ~$100 today.

## Supervised Fine-Tuning: Teaching via example
**Humans set the personality.** ChatGPT = statistical simulation of OpenAI's data labelers following labeling instructions. When you talk to it, you're essentially asking: "What would a hired expert say here?" It's not magic; it's imitation of ~1 million curated human conversations.

**System prompts are invisible tokens.** Behind every ChatGPT response, hidden tokens pre-pended to the context tell the model "You are ChatGPT, trained by OpenAI, knowledge cutoff April 2024." These shape all downstream tokens. Without them, the model calls itself GPT-2 (because pre-training saw more OpenAI references online).

**Hallucinations are structural.** Base models predict the next token; they don't know unknowns, so they guess confidently and invent facts. Meta's mitigation: probe what models actually know, then add training data where the correct answer is "I don't know." Works because models have some internal signal of uncertainty; fine-tuning teaches them to voice it.

## Reinforcement Learning: Discovery, not imitation
**Emergent reasoning discovered, not taught.** When trained with RL on math/code problems with verifiable answers, models spontaneously discover chains of thought—backtracking, reconsidering steps, trying multiple approaches—no human labeled these. Deep Seek R1 showed response length bloats 10x because the model learns that "thinking out loud" improves accuracy. This is move 37: strategies no human would play.

**Mental arithmetic fails unless spread across tokens.** Models can't crunch 23×177 in one forward pass (fixed compute budget). Ask for the answer directly: wrong. Ask for intermediate steps (Emily bought 3 apples..., each orange is $2..., total cost minus oranges = ..., each apple = $3): correct. Or use code interpreter—models write Python, Python runs it, model sees result. Counting requires code too.

**RLHF is fine-tuning, not real RL.** "Reinforcement learning from human feedback" trains a reward model to simulate human preferences (jokes, poems). But run it 1000 steps and it games the simulator—nonsensical outputs score perfectly. You stop training after ~200 steps. Math RL never tops out because correct answers can't be faked. This is why reasoning models (O3, DeepSeek R1) exist only for verifiable domains; creativity still uses supervised fine-tuning.

## Critical gaps (the Swiss cheese)
**Context length = thinking budget.** GPT-2: 1,024 tokens context. Modern: 200,000+. More context = more space for intermediate reasoning. Without it, models skip mental steps and guess.

**Spelling breaks due to tokenization.** "How many Rs in strawberry?" fails because models see tokens, not letters. Combined with inability to count, this is a hole in capability that seems absurd given they solve PhD physics problems.

**9.11 vs 9.9 randomly fails.** Bible verse tokenization (9:11, 9:9) confuses models; neurons fire for religious-text patterns even in math. No one fully understands this glitch. Check their work.

## Practical upshot
**Use them as tools, not oracles.** For factual queries, paste the document into the context window (working memory) rather than relying on parameters (vague recollection). Ask for code execution on arithmetic. Use thinking models (O3, DeepSeek R1) for reasoning problems; use standard models for faster knowledge queries. Verify everything.

**Current frontier.** Thinking models are primordial—RL reasoning is weeks old in production. Expect multimodal (vision + audio native in one model), long-running agents (hours-long tasks with human supervision), and test-time learning (models updating parameters during inference, not just at training).

title: Why Is the Sky Blue? 🌌 The Science Behind It Explained! #Shorts #Science
text: The sky is blue because blue light from sunlight has a shorter wavelength, and atmospheric molecules like nitrogen and oxygen scatter short-wavelength light much more strongly than longer wavelengths. This scattered blue light reaches your eyes from all directions across the sky. At sunset, sunlight travels through much more atmosphere, so blue light gets scattered away further, leaving red and orange wavelengths to reach your eyes instead.

title: Do Things that Don't Scale
text: Startups succeed by doing unscalable, manually labor-intensive work early on: recruiting users individually rather than waiting for them to arrive, delighting them with extraordinary attention (like hand-written thank you notes), focusing initially on a narrow market to build critical mass, and sometimes manually delivering services before automating. Founders resist this because it seems too small to matter and because they underestimate compound growth—but 10% weekly user growth becomes 2 million users in two years. The feedback loop from direct user engagement shapes the actual product better than any initial plan, and these early practices should become permanent parts of company culture. Big launches, partnerships, and other passive strategies don't work as shortcuts; you have to make an extraordinary effort in both the product and the unscalable customer engagement.
name: plain blog post (Paul Graham)

title: Do Things that Don't Scale
text:
**Startups don't grow by making something great and waiting for demand. Founders must manually recruit users one by one and obsess over their experience—counterintuitively, these labor-intensive tasks become permanent strengths.**

**Growth math**: 10% weekly growth from 100 users yields 14,000 after a year, 2 million after two. That's why the first step of recruiting 10 users matters despite seeming inconsequential.

**Stripe's "Collison installation"**: Most beta users got a link. Patrick and John Collison would demand "Give me your laptop" and set them up live on the spot. Obsessive manual setup became their recruiting method.

**Airbnb's 30-day escape hatch**: The founders traveled door-to-door in NYC recruiting users and fixing host listings. Graham notes they arrived at YC dinners with rolly bags because they were constantly flying somewhere. That month of in-person engagement made the difference between success and failure—the company was that fragile.

**Bill Gates returned to Harvard**: He took a semester after starting Microsoft because he didn't realize it would become important. Inexperienced founders constantly underestimate their own startups; you must push back against your own skepticism.

**Manual ops disguised as features**: Stripe gave users "instant" merchant accounts by manually signing them up for traditional accounts behind the scenes. Viaweb built e-commerce stores for merchants by hand before automating; in the process, they discovered what merchants actually needed. Pebble assembled watches themselves before Kickstarter; when they finally mass-produced, they'd learned lessons (like sourcing good screws) they'd never have discovered from a factory.

**Facebook started narrow**: Just Harvard students—a few thousand market. Zuckerberg manually created course lists for each school to make students feel it was *their* natural home. Only after critical mass did he expand to other colleges, then everywhere.

**Why big launches flop**: Founders believe broadcasting their existence will bring users. Actually, novel things take time to reach people's attention. The launches people remember are famous failures (Segway, Google Wave).

**The "insanely great" trap**: Steve Jobs meant obsessive design quality on the Mac. Early-stage founders misread this as "build a perfect product." Actually, it means deliver an insanely great *user experience* with a buggy product—make up the gap with attentiveness. A hand-written thank-you note (Wufoo's tactic) and perfect setup (Stripe) matter more than polish.

**Ben Silbermann found his vector**: Pinterest's early users were interested in design. Instead of waiting for organic growth, he went to a design blogger conference to recruit deliberately. This works because early adopters reveal which subset of the market will take off.

**Think of startups as vectors, not scalars**: A startup is (1) what you build *plus* (2) the specific unscalable thing you do to launch it. Founders who skip the second part—expecting partnerships or launches to do the work—fail. The unscalable part often becomes permanent culture: if you're aggressive recruiting users at 10, you'll be aggressive at 10,000.
